entries.short: ISK (interstellar kredits) is EVE Online's primary in-game currency.
entries.longer: ISK is earned through missions, mining, trading, manufacturing, and countless other activities, and spent on ships, modules, skillbooks, and market fees. It has no fixed real-world value, but PLEX creates an informal ISK-to-real-money exchange rate through the market.

entries.short: PLEX (Pilot's License Extension) is a tradeable item that pays for game time, in-game store purchases, or can be sold to other players for ISK.
entries.longer: CCP sells PLEX for real money; players can redeem it for 30 days of Omega subscription time, spend it in the in-game store, or sell it on the market for ISK, which is how most players fund subscriptions and cosmetics without paying twice.

entries.short: High-security space: systems with a security status of 0.5 or above, where CONCORD punishes unlawful aggression within seconds.
entries.longer: In hisec, CONCORD (an NPC police force) destroys ships that attack other players without a legal reason (a war, or a suspect/criminal flag) very quickly, though it cannot prevent the first hit — which is how a gank fleet can still kill an unsuspecting hauler before CONCORD arrives.

entries.short: Low-security space: systems with a security status from 0.1 to 0.4, where CONCORD does not intervene but faction police may still punish criminals.
entries.longer: Lowsec sits between hisec and nullsec: players can freely engage each other without CONCORD retaliation, faction police only attack players with very negative security status, and gates aren't camped by NPCs — only by other players.

entries.short: Null-security space: systems with a security status of 0.0 or below, where CONCORD and faction police do not operate at all.
entries.longer: Nullsec is largely player-controlled through sovereignty and is where the biggest fleet battles, richest resources, and highest risks in the game are found; short of the game's own rules, anything goes.

entries.short: An unprovoked, deliberately fatal attack on another player's ship, usually in hisec, accepting CONCORD's retaliation as a cost of doing business.
entries.longer: A "suicide gank" sacrifices the attacker's own ship (which CONCORD destroys moments after the kill) to destroy a much more valuable target — typically an AFK miner or a hauler carrying valuable cargo. Newbies most often meet ganking as the reason a seemingly "safe" hisec belt or trade route wasn't safe at all.

entries.short: The primary faster-than-light travel method within a single solar system, used to move between celestial objects, gates, and bookmarks.
entries.longer: A ship must align to its destination and accelerate to 75% of its maximum velocity before it can enter warp; once warping it is untargetable, then decelerates on arrival. Warp is always intra-system — moving between systems requires a stargate jump (or, for capitals, a jump drive).

entries.short: The time a ship takes to accelerate to 75% of its top speed before it can enter warp.
entries.longer: Align time is set by a ship's mass and agility (inertia modifier), and is the main number newbies should watch when fitting for survivability: a fast-aligning ship spends less time vulnerable on grid before escaping into warp. "Insta-align" colloquially means aligning in about 2 seconds or less.

entries.short: The directional scanner: a built-in ship instrument that detects ships, structures, drones, and wrecks up to 14 AU away in a chosen direction.
entries.longer: Dscan cannot see cloaked ships and doesn't give exact distances or bearings without narrowing the scan angle, but it's the cheapest, most-used situational-awareness tool in the game — pilots check it constantly before undocking, warping, or engaging.

entries.short: An automatically generated record of a ship's destruction, showing the victim, attackers, location, time, fit, and estimated ISK value lost.
entries.longer: Killmails are the basic unit of combat evidence in EVE — sites like zKillboard aggregate them for public viewing, and EVE Assist's planned loss-autopsy feature reads a killmail to explain in plain language what killed you and why.

entries.short: A backup body stored at a station that lets a pilot instantly relocate their consciousness there, skipping travel time.
entries.longer: Jumping to a clone keeps your skills and standings but leaves your current ship, items, and any implants behind (fitted to whichever clone you leave). It's commonly used to stage in a remote region or to protect an expensive implant set from being lost with a pod.

entries.short: The ordered list of skills a character is currently training, processed one after another in real time even while offline.
entries.longer: Training happens continuously as long as the queue isn't empty (Omega characters can queue skills far in advance; Alpha clones have shorter queue limits), so keeping the queue filled is one of the simplest ways to make steady long-term progress.

entries.short: A standardized ship type and fit that fleet members are asked to bring, so a fleet fights as a predictable, complementary unit.
entries.longer: Doctrines let a fleet commander plan tactics around known damage types, ranges, and roles instead of a random mix of ships, and let corporations bulk-buy or reimburse a small set of hulls rather than everything members might otherwise fly.

entries.short: Leaving a station (or, for player structures, an Upwell citadel) and returning to open space.
entries.longer: Undocking ends station invulnerability immediately; ships spawn along a fixed vector outside the station and are vulnerable to anything already waiting there, which is why checking dscan and local before undocking in dangerous space is standard practice.

entries.short: A trading strategy that buys and resells items within a single station, profiting from the spread between buy and sell orders without hauling anything.
entries.longer: It requires no travel risk, just patience, market fees (broker fee and sales tax), and enough capital and order slots to keep multiple items working at once — a common first trading strategy for newbies based near a major hub.

entries.short: The largest named subdivision of New Eden's map, made up of multiple constellations, each containing multiple solar systems.
entries.longer: Regions are the unit most market and logistics tools (including EVE Assist's market tools) report prices and routes by; New Eden spans thousands of star systems with stargate connections across dozens of regions of varying security.

entries.short: Traveling from one solar system to an adjacent one through a stargate.
entries.longer: Arriving at a gate always drops a ship out of warp at range, and after jumping there is a short forced invulnerability ("gate cloak") until the ship moves or takes an action — the classic moment gate camps wait to strike.

entries.short: A group of hostile ships stationed at a stargate, waiting to tackle and destroy whoever jumps through.
entries.longer: Camps are most common on well-traveled lowsec and nullsec routes; scouting ahead, checking dscan on arrival, and having an instant-align escape plan are the standard countermeasures. EVE Assist's system-activity tool is meant to help spot recent kill activity that hints at a camp before you jump in.

entries.short: The capsule a pilot's consciousness rides in — and controls the ship through — once their ship is destroyed.
entries.longer: A pod is fast to lose and carries no combat capability; being "podded" (having the pod itself destroyed) is what actually kills the current clone and any implants fitted to it, which is why many pilots warp their pod away the instant their ship dies.

entries.short: The paid subscription state, which unlocks training and use of every skill in the game.
entries.longer: Omega time can be bought with real money or with PLEX bought from other players, and is required for some high-end activities (capital ships, certain skill levels) that Alpha clones cannot access at all.

entries.short: The permanently free-to-play state, with a restricted set of trainable skills and lower skill point gain.
entries.longer: Alpha is not a time-limited trial — it's playable indefinitely — but several ship classes, skill levels, and activities are Omega-only, so most committed players eventually subscribe.

entries.short: Scrap components pulled from wrecks after a ship is destroyed, used to build rigs and other items.
entries.longer: Salvaging requires a salvager module and, usually, a tractor beam to pull wrecks into range; it's a low-skill, relatively safe way for newbies to earn ISK from wrecks left behind by mission runners or ratters.

entries.short: Slang for an NPC pirate or monster encountered in space, most often in asteroid belts, missions, or combat sites.
entries.longer: "Ratting" means killing rats for bounties and loot; belt rats are the small, low-threat spawns newbies meet first, while mission and nullsec rats scale up to genuinely dangerous NPC fleets.

entries.short: A player who repeatedly accepts and completes agent missions for ISK, standings, and loyalty points.
entries.longer: Missions are private PvE combat, courier, or trade tasks offered by NPC agents at stations; running them is one of the most structured, low-risk income sources for a new character.

entries.short: A dedicated mining ship class (Procurer, Retriever, Covetor) with much larger ore holds and mining bonuses than a mining frigate.
entries.longer: Barges trade combat capability and speed for yield and cargo, and their upgraded versions ("exhumers") push that further still; because they're slow and often flown semi-AFK, they're a classic gank target in hisec.

entries.short: A cheap, fast, Alpha-friendly mining frigate with an extra ore hold, mining bonuses, and a built-in resistance to being warp scrambled.
entries.longer: It's usually the first mining ship a new player flies, before graduating to a mining barge, thanks to its low cost and forgiving fit.

entries.short: The smallest ship class: cheap, fast, and agile, used for tackle, exploration, early combat, and mining (Venture).
entries.longer: Frigates are the standard first combat ship for new pilots — inexpensive enough to lose without financial pain while learning the game's mechanics.

entries.short: A ship class one size above frigates, trading some agility for extra turret/launcher slots and burst damage.
entries.longer: Destroyers are popular for cheap, high-DPS PvP fits and early mission running; specialized subtypes (command destroyers, tactical destroyers) add mobility or role-swapping tricks.

entries.short: A mid-size ship class balancing tank, damage, and cost, used across mining, mission running, exploration, and PvP doctrines.
entries.longer: Cruisers are usually a new pilot's step up once frigates and destroyers feel limiting, and remain relevant throughout the game via specialized variants (Heavy Assault Cruisers, Strategic Cruisers, and more).

entries.short: The NPC police force that punishes unlawful aggression in high-security space, usually by destroying the attacker within seconds.
entries.longer: CONCORD cannot prevent the first shot, only retaliate afterward — the loophole suicide ganks exploit — and it has no authority (and does not respond) in lowsec or nullsec.

entries.short: A temporary flag that keeps a player "in combat" — vulnerable to further attack and unable to dock or jump safely for a period after fighting.
entries.longer: EVE layers several such timers (weapons timer, criminal timer, and others) depending on what happened and where; the practical takeaway for newbies is: if you've recently fought or been aggressed, don't assume you can dock or warp away consequence-free.

entries.short: A per-character setting (green/yellow/red) that restricts which of your own actions the client will let you take, to prevent accidental illegal or hostile actions.
entries.longer: On green safety you cannot accidentally shoot another player or steal from their wreck in a way that would flag you as a criminal; lowering it to yellow or red is a deliberate choice to allow riskier or more aggressive actions.

entries.short: A system where paying an upfront premium on a ship's hull refunds part of its value in ISK if it's destroyed.
entries.longer: Insurance only covers the base hull, never fitted modules or cargo, and payouts scale with the coverage tier purchased; it softens, but never eliminates, the ISK cost of a loss.

entries.short: A player-created, formal agreement to exchange items, ISK, or courier services, enforced by the game rather than trust.
entries.longer: Contract types include item exchange (a fixed-price sale, including bundles the market can't handle), auctions, and courier contracts, each visible only to the parties or public region the creator chooses.

entries.short: A contract that pays a hauler to move cargo from one location to another, backed by a collateral deposit.
entries.longer: The requester sets a reward and a collateral amount; if the hauler fails to deliver within the deadline, the requester keeps the collateral instead of the goods, which is what makes hiring a stranger to haul your items viable.

entries.short: A standing offer to buy (buy order) or sell (sell order) a specific item at a specific price, posted at a station or structure's market.
entries.longer: Orders sit on the regional market until filled, expire, or are canceled; EVE Assist's market tools read these public order books to find best prices, compare hubs, and watch for undercuts.

entries.short: A percentage fee charged when placing a market order, whether or not it ever fills.
entries.longer: The base rate (around 3% at NPC stations) is reduced by standings and the Broker Relations skill; it's paid up front, unlike sales tax, which is only paid on a completed sale.

entries.short: A percentage fee taken from the proceeds of a completed sell order.
entries.longer: The base rate is 7.5%, reduced by the Accounting skill and by standings; together with the broker fee it's the main cost of doing business as a trader, and the two combined are why "buy low, sell high" margins need to clear a real threshold to be profitable.

entries.short: A -10 to +10 score representing how favorably an NPC corporation, faction, or agent regards a character.
entries.longer: Higher standings unlock better mission agents, lower broker fees and sales tax, and reduce how aggressively faction police react to a character's security status; standings are raised mainly by running missions and completing agent tasks for that faction.

entries.short: An NPC that offers missions and, for research agents, research points, usually stationed at a specific station.
entries.longer: Agents are ranked level 1 through 5 by difficulty/reward and gated by the standing a character has with their corporation or faction; running an agent's missions raises that standing over time, unlocking higher-level agents.

entries.short: Loyalty points: a faction-specific currency earned mainly from missions, redeemable at that faction's LP store for ships, modules, blueprints, and other items.
entries.longer: LP has no direct ISK value — its worth depends entirely on what the issuing corporation's LP store sells and what those items resell for on the market — so "ISK per LP" is a common way traders and mission runners evaluate which agent to run.

entries.short: An unstable, randomly-connected passage between two systems, including systems in wormhole space (W-space) that don't appear on the normal star map.
entries.longer: Wormholes have a mass limit and a lifespan before collapsing, no local chat showing who's in system, and their own security quirks, making them a higher-risk, higher-reward environment popular with small, self-sufficient groups.

entries.short: A temporary, high-value PvE invasion by the Sansha's Nation faction into a constellation, fought by player fleets for large ISK rewards.
entries.longer: Incursions form organically across New Eden, move between constellations over their lifespan, and are typically run by structured, high-DPS/high-logistics community fleets rather than solo players.

entries.short: Short for abyssal deadspace: a solo, instanced PvE pocket entered with an Abyssal Filament, containing escalating combat rooms and environmental hazards, with a strict time limit to escape.
entries.longer: Abyssal running rewards mutated modules and materials but is unforgiving of mistakes — there's no calling for help and no leaving early without losing the loot, so ships are usually fit specifically for it.

entries.short: An opt-in, low-stakes war between the four empire factions that lets players fight over system control and earn LP for kills and objectives.
entries.longer: Joining locks a character to one side's militia, changes standings toward the opposing empires, and opens faction warfare complexes and LP rewards as an accessible entry point into large-scale PvP.

entries.short: Short for sovereignty: the system by which a player alliance claims and holds ownership of nullsec systems, usually via structures like the Sovereignty Hub.
entries.longer: Holding sov grants access to that system's resources and upgrades but requires ongoing structure defense and activity, which is why sovereignty warfare is one of the largest organized activities in the game.

entries.short: A formal grouping of multiple corporations under a shared banner, usually for coordinated nullsec, wormhole, or large-scale PvP play.
entries.longer: Alliances share standings toward other alliances (wars, blues, enemies) and often share sovereignty, doctrines, and infrastructure across their member corporations.

entries.short: A player-run organization — EVE's equivalent of a guild — that members join for shared goals, infrastructure, and a group of people to play with.
entries.longer: Corporations range from small newbie-friendly groups to large nullsec power blocs; EVE University itself, the source of much of this glossary, is a corporation focused on teaching new players.

entries.short: A temporary group of pilots operating together under a fleet commander, with shared broadcasts, waypoints, and squad/wing structure.
entries.longer: Fleets range from a two-person mining op to hundred-plus-pilot nullsec battles; joining one is usually the fastest way for a newbie to safely experience higher-risk content.

entries.short: The specific combination of modules, rigs, and ammo/drones loaded onto a ship for a given role.
entries.longer: A fit determines what a ship can actually do — its tank, damage, speed, and utility — and is usually the first thing more experienced players will ask about or critique when reviewing a loss or a plan.

entries.short: A ship's ability to survive incoming damage, achieved by boosting and/or repairing one of its three defense pools: shield, armor, or hull.
entries.longer: "Buffer tanking" stacks raw hitpoints to survive burst damage; "active tanking" repairs damage in real time to survive sustained fights. Most ships are built to tank primarily through one layer while treating the others as backup.

entries.short: A tanking approach that boosts and/or actively repairs a ship's shield, its outermost and (for most races) primary defense layer.
entries.longer: Shield modules fit in the mid slots and typically don't compete with a ship's damage-dealing high or low slots, which is why Caldari and Minmatar ships are traditionally built around shield tanking.

entries.short: A tanking approach that boosts and/or actively repairs a ship's armor layer, beneath its shield.
entries.longer: Armor modules fit in the low slots, competing with damage and fitting modules for the same slots — the classic trade-off Amarr and Gallente ships (traditionally armor-tanked) are built around.

entries.short: Relying on a ship's raw structural hitpoints as its last line of defense, after shield and armor are exhausted.
entries.longer: Very few fits tank primarily through the hull on purpose — it's mostly a last-resort buffer — though a handful of niche fits (and desperate last stands) deliberately stack bulkheads and hull hitpoints.

entries.short: A ship's onboard energy reserve, drained by most active modules (guns, repairers, propulsion) and recharged passively over time.
entries.longer: Running out of capacitor ("cap out") shuts down active modules until it recovers, which is why capacitor management — and capacitor warfare, which drains an enemy's cap remotely — is a core part of both PvE and PvP fitting.

entries.short: An item fitted into one of a ship's high, mid, or low slots that changes what the ship can do.
entries.longer: Modules range from weapons and repairers to propulsion, electronic warfare, and utility systems; the full set fitted to a ship is its fitting, and figuring out how much of a ship's power grid/CPU/capacitor it costs is most of what fitting a ship involves.

entries.short: A permanent, non-removable upgrade fitted into a ship's rig slots, usually trading a drawback (like reduced cargo or targeting range) for a significant bonus.
entries.longer: Because rigs are destroyed (not returned) when unfit, they represent a more committed choice than regular modules, and are commonly used to specialize a hull for one role — a mining ship's ore hold, a combat ship's tank, and so on.

entries.short: A small robotic ship launched from a ship's drone bay to fight, mine, salvage, or provide other support autonomously.
entries.longer: Drones are directed to attack, mine, or return to bay by their pilot but act somewhat independently once launched, and are a major part of Gallente ship design in particular.

entries.short: Consumable charges loaded into turrets or missile launchers that determine a weapon's damage type, range, and tracking.
entries.longer: Each weapon system has its own family of ammunition — projectile ammunition for autocannons/artillery, hybrid charges for blasters/railguns, crystals for lasers, and missiles/rockets for launchers — with cheaper tiers trading damage for lower cost and higher tiers doing the reverse.

entries.short: Using modules like warp scramblers, disruptors, or webs to stop a target from warping away or slow it down.
entries.longer: A dedicated "tackler" — often a fast, cheap frigate — holds a target in place until the rest of the fleet arrives, making tackle one of the most valuable and lowest-cost roles a newbie can fly in a fleet.

entries.short: A module that prevents its target from entering warp and, on most ships, also disables microwarpdrives.
entries.longer: It has shorter range than a warp disruptor and stacks with other scrambling effects; escaping one usually requires more warp-core-stabilizing strength than the attacker has scramble strength, or destroying/outlasting the tackler.

entries.short: Short for cynosural field: a beacon effect that lights up a temporary jump-in point other ships can jump to.
entries.longer: Lighting a cyno announces your location to everyone in the system and is how capital fleets deploy or "lightspeed" ships in via jump portals; because it's so visible, cyno lighting is a common bait/trap tactic in null-sec and low-sec warfare.

entries.short: The largest and most expensive player-flyable ship class, capable of fitting a doomsday superweapon and, on most titans, generating jump bridges for a fleet.
entries.longer: Titans anchor major nullsec fleet battles and are a primary target/prize in them; losing one is a headline-level event precisely because of the enormous ISK and organizational investment they represent.
